shortTheory.question: Enlist the events that occur during the G1 phase of interphase.
shortTheory.answer: During this phase cell makes proteins and organelles and so grows in size. Cell also makes enzymes that are required in S phase for the replication of DNA.

shortTheory.question: What is the main purpose of the S phase in the cell cycle?
shortTheory.answer: During this phase, the DNA of each chromosome is replicated (copied). It results in the duplication of chromosomes (each chromosome consists of two sister chromatids). The total number of chromosomes in cell remains the same.

shortTheory.question: How does crossing over contribute to genetic variation in meiosis?
shortTheory.answer: Crossing over creates new combinations of genes on chromosomes. Each chromosome in the gametes carries a unique set of genes.

shortTheory.question: What is the role of spindle fibres in mitosis?
shortTheory.answer: The spindle fibres attached with chromosomes pull toward the poles. Due to this pulling, the chromosome's sister chromatids separate.

shortTheory.question: How is cytokinesis in animal cell different from plant cell?
shortTheory.answer: In animal cells, a furrow develops in the cell membrane at the equator. At this furrow, the cytoplasm has a ring of microfilaments. The ring contracts and the furrow moves inward. In this way parent cell is pinched into two. In plant cells, Golgi apparatus makes vesicles. These vesicles move to the middle and fuse to form a plate called phragmoplast. The plate grows outward and its membranes fuse with the cell membrane. The result is two daughter cells.

shortTheory.question: What are sister chromatids, and when do they separate in meiosis?
shortTheory.answer: Each chromosome consists of two sister chromatids. In anaphase-II, spindle fibres pull sister chromatids apart toward opposite poles.

definitions.text: It is the series of events that take place in a eukaryotic cell from its formation to its division into two daughter cells.
Many cells stop dividing and start performing their specific functions. This phase is called G0 phase.
Mitosis is the type of cell division in which a cell divides into two daughter cells, each with the same number of chromosomes as were present in the parent cell.
Karyokinesis means the division of the nucleus.
It is the division of cytoplasm.
It is the type of cell division in which each daughter cell receives half the number of chromosomes as compared to the parent cell.
Diploid means the cells in which chromosomes are in pairs (homologous pairs)
haploid means the cells with half number of chromosomes i.e., cells with no pairs of chromosomes.
They pair up in a process called synapsis.
Each pair of homologous chromosomes is called tetrad.
Each chiasma is the site for crossing over i.e., exchange of portions of chromosomes between non-sister chromatids.
During meiosis-I, chromosomes separate while during meiosis-II sister chromatids separate. It is called disjunction.
Sometimes non-disjunction occurs. Due to it, the daughter cells (gametes) receive more or less than the normal number of chromosomes.
Due to this uncontrolled division, masses of cells are formed. These masses are called tumors.
If the tumors remain in their original location, they are called benign.
If they migrate and invade other tissues, they are called malignant tumors (cancer).
It is called metastasis(spreading of disease).

fullMarks: For a mitosis or meiosis question, write the stages in the correct order and give a separate, clear point for each stage.
In mitosis answers, distinguish karyokinesis (nuclear division) from cytokinesis (cytoplasm division); do not leave cytokinesis out.
For meiosis-I, state that homologous chromosomes pair and crossing over occurs in prophase-I, then separate in anaphase-I while sister chromatids remain together.
For a mitosis-versus-meiosis comparison, use paired points and clearly compare number of divisions, number of daughter cells, chromosome number and crossing over.
When describing animal and plant cytokinesis, name the animal cleavage furrow and the plant cell plate/phragmoplast, and explain how each forms.

For significance questions, use clear headings such as growth, cell replacement, regeneration and asexual reproduction for mitosis; explain chromosome-number maintenance and genetic diversity for meiosis.
Draw a large, neat, correctly sequenced diagram when asked; label chromosomes, spindle fibres, poles, equator and any relevant structures such as chiasmata or the cell plate.

mistakes: Mistake: Saying that DNA replication doubles the chromosome number in S phase. Fix: State that DNA is copied and each chromosome has two sister chromatids, but the total number of chromosomes remains the same.
Mistake: Saying sister chromatids separate in anaphase-I. Fix: In anaphase-I homologous chromosomes separate; sister chromatids separate in anaphase-II.
Mistake: Confusing homologous chromosomes with sister chromatids. Fix: Homologous chromosomes pair in prophase-I; sister chromatids are the two copies joined at one centromere.
Mistake: Describing plant cytokinesis as a cleavage furrow. Fix: Animal cells form a furrow; plant cells form a cell plate from vesicles.
Mistake: Writing that crossing over happens in mitosis. Fix: Identify crossing over as an event of prophase-I of meiosis.
Mistake: Listing mitosis stages but forgetting cytokinesis. Fix: After telophase, state how the cytoplasm divides to produce two daughter cells.
